evidence.title: Inflammatory Bowel Competitive Landscape Analysis 2026 | Eureka
evidence.text: Notably, 2025-2026 has produced an exceptional wave of approvals including Janssen’s oral peptide IL-23 antagonist Icotrokinra (March 2026), Lilly’s Mirikizumab (Omvoh) for Crohn’s expansion, and multiple Chinese-developed JAK and IL-23 mAb approvals. Specifically, the late-stage IBD landscape is bifurcated between injectable biologics — AbbVie’s Skyrizi (Risankizumab) and Rinvoq (Upadacitinib), Janssen’s Stelara (Ustekinumab) and Tremfya (Guselkumab), Takeda’s Entyvio (Vedolizumab), Pfizer’s Etrasimod (Velsipity), and BMS’s Zeposia (Ozanimod) — and the emerging oral biologic and JAK1-selective wave. Moreover, sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) modulators have established a third oral mechanism alongside JAK and TYK2 inhibitors. However, the strategic outlook is increasingly defined by oral peptide IL-23 antagonists and selective JAK1 inhibitors rather than next-generation TNF or anti-integrin biologics. ... Furthermore, microbiome therapeutics, mesenchymal stem cell therapy, and IL-23 / TL1A combination biology extend the long-term modality horizon. ... Across the 200 sampled IBD programs, small molecules dominate with 114 entries (oral JAK, TYK2, S1P modulators), followed by 31 monoclonal antibodies, 6 herbal medicines, 4 mesenchymal stem cell therapies, 3 synthetic peptides, 3 cyclic peptides, 3 bispecific antibodies, 3 probiotics, and 3 polymers. Notably, the strong small-molecule presence reflects oral therapy ambitions across multiple mechanisms.

evidence.title: Competitor Landscape
evidence.text: The regulatory approval of next-generation biologics targeting novel inflammatory pathways - including JAK inhibitors, integrin antagonists, and S1P receptor modulators - has substantially broadened the therapeutic arsenal. ... The therapeutic landscape for inflammatory bowel disease has undergone revolutionary transformation through emergence of mechanistically distinct biologic classes offering superior efficacy and safety profiles compared to conventional small-molecule immunosuppressants. JAK-STAT inhibitors including tofacitinib and upadacitinib demonstrate oral bioavailability combined with targeted intracellular signaling inhibition, achieving clinical remission rates of 48-56% in moderate-to-severe disease compared to 22-28% with conventional therapies. Integrin antagonists such as vedolizumab provide selective gut-homing lymphocyte targeting, substantially reducing systemic immunosuppression and opportunistic infection risk. Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators represent an emerging frontier, with ozanimod demonstrating 41% remission rates while preserving systemic immunity. Furthermore, dual-mechanism agents combining TNF inhibition with IL-23 pathway targeting are entering late-stage development, with interim data suggesting remission rates exceeding 58-62% in treatment-naive cohorts. ... Biologic therapies including TNF inhibitors, integrin antagonists, IL-12/IL-23 inhibitors, and JAK inhibitors represent the most rapidly expanding therapeutic category, driven by superior efficacy profiles enabling disease remission in 45-65% of patients compared to 20-35% with conventional small-molecule therapies. ... Integrin antagonist vedolizumab commands 18.7% of biologic market revenues, offering gut-selective targeting advantages particularly appealing to patients with treatment-limiting infections or malignancy concerns. ... Patients presenting with pure colonic ulcerative colitis frequently receive integrin antagonists or JAK inhibitors as first-line biologic therapy, leveraging gut-selective mechanisms minimizing systemic immunosuppression.

The overall safety profile was favourable and consistent with that of guselkumab in approved indications. output.summarized_answer: Bezlotoxumab (Zinplava; CDB1) is the named anti-TcdB monoclonal-antibody comparator. It binds two epitopes in the TcdB CROPS near the hinge, whereas AZD5148 binds the TcdB glucosyltransferase domain (GTD); the reported epitope conservation was 82.47% for bezlotoxumab and 99.58% for AZD5148 across 9,134 global isolates. Bezlotoxumab was approved as a single intravenous infusion of 10 mg/kg in the USA and European Union to prevent recurrent CDI in high-risk people receiving antibacterial treatment; its production was discontinued in January 2025. [E1][E2][E3][E4][E5] AZD5148, formerly PA41, is an anti-TcdB humanized monoclonal antibody that blocks delivery of the GTD enzymatic cargo into host-cell cytosol. It has a YTE Fc substitution (M252Y/S254T/T256E), and the stated strategy targets the GTD independently of the target cell’s receptor. [E1][E3][E4][E5] In vitro, AZD5148 neutralized TcdB1 and TcdB2 with EC50 values 1,000- to 14,000-fold lower than bezlotoxumab and neutralized eight recent circulating TcdB ribotypes; in mouse CDI models it protected against weight loss and mortality at significantly lower doses than bezlotoxumab. It also conferred protection in a gnotobiotic piglet CDI model and mouse models involving different TcdB ribotypes. Adding anti-TcdA mAb PA50 provided no additional protective benefit in the reported mouse study. [E3][E4][E5] AstraZeneca’s H1/Q2 2026 appendix lists AZD5148’s Phase IIb PRISM study, NCT07285213, in 230 adults with a qualifying CDI episode: randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled, with AZD5148 or placebo, primary endpoint efficacy, secondary endpoints safety and pharmacokinetics, first-patient-clinical-dose in Q4 2025, and data anticipated after 2027. [E7] The appendix also lists Phase I NCT06469151 in 84 healthy volunteers as randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose escalation: cohort 1 received dose 1 intramuscularly; cohorts 2a and 2b dose 2 intramuscularly, with cohort 2b Chinese participants; cohort 3 dose 2 intravenously; cohorts 4a and 4b dose 3 intravenously, with cohort 4b Chinese participants; and cohort 5 dose 4 intravenously. Its primary endpoint was safety, secondary endpoint pharmacokinetic parameters, first patient in Q2 2024, last patient in Q4 2024, and data readout Q1 2026. [E7] A 2025 profile lists three active clinical trials: D8820C00005, Phase I, active but not recruiting, for Clostridium infections, with primary completion 2025-12-29 and a 69% probability of success; jRCT2071240071, Phase I, not yet recruiting, in healthy volunteers, with primary completion 2026-01-12; and D8820C00002, Phase I, active but not recruiting, in healthy volunteers, with primary completion 2025-11-07 and a 69% probability of success. [E6] The evidence gives no support for the stated episode criterion of receipt of fidaxomicin, vancomycin or metronidazole with a planned 10–25-day duration at IMP administration, or for whether that criterion applies to PRISM. It also does not give bezlotoxumab’s trial registry, enrolment, endpoint results or development stage, or profiles/results for any other same-class competing agents. [E1][E2][E3][E4][E5][E6][E7]

Early disease patients also experienced significantly fewer serious adverse events. ... SOR102 is an oral bispecific antibody targeting TNF and IL-23p19 developed for ulcer ative colitis. This phase 1, double blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated its safety, pharmacokinetics, and preliminary efficacy in healthy participants and patients with active ulcerative colitis. Across single and multiple ascending doses, SOR102 was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate adverse events and no clinically significant safety signals. In patients with ulcerative colitis treated for 42 days, clinical responses were more frequent with SOR102 than placebo, particularly with twice-daily dosing. Symptomatic remission was achieved in over half of patients receiving twice-daily SOR102, while no placebo-treated patients reached remission. Although one severe disease exacerbation occurred, it was not considered treatment related. Overall, the favourable safety profile and early signs of clinical bene fit support further clinical development of SOR102 as a potential oral therapy for ulcerative colitis.
